overview: This bill would require the Secretary of Commerce to set up a National Manufacturing Advisory Council within the Commerce Department within 180 days. The council of up to 30 members, drawn from industry (including small and mid-sized manufacturers), academia and labor, would meet at least twice a year to advise the government on manufacturing issues such as worker training, supply chain disruptions, new technology and regulations that raise costs. It would produce a yearly national strategic plan for manufacturing and send it to the Secretary and Congress. The council would take over the work of the existing U.S. Manufacturing Council and would end about five years after its first meeting. No new money is authorized for it. The Senate passed it, and as of July 15, 2025, it was being held at the desk in the House awaiting action.
for: Supporters say it gives manufacturers and workers a permanent, organized voice in federal policy and a yearly plan for keeping U.S. manufacturing competitive, without new spending.
against: Critics say it largely rebrands an advisory group that already exists, and advisory councils often produce reports that have little effect on actual policy.
